still_true: Wegovy's US list price is still $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The FDA has approved no generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US. Exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32, and generic liraglutide is still the only generic incretin on the US market.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, and oral Wegovy starting doses still cost $149 a month there.
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly are still the only sellers of branded incretins in the US. Lilly still leads on efficacy.

The suicidal-ideation warning the FDA asked to have removed in January 2026 is still off the Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels, and the 503B compounding exclusion proposed in April 2026 was finalised and still stands.

population.note: FICTIONAL estimates. Arithmetic: 22.0% ever-used minus 16.3% current = 5.7% of adults who have used the drugs and are off them now. 40% of ever-users have cycled, which is 8.8 points: about 7.5 points are current users on at least their second course (46% of current users), and about 1.3 points are people who cycled before and are off again. That fits roughly one-third persistence at one year and 36–47% restarting within a year, compounded over several cycles. About 16.3% of ~265M adults is ~43M current users. FICTIONAL payer mix: commercial ~33% (~14M), Medicare ~19% (~8M, mostly diabetes, cardiovascular and kidney codes after the pilot ended), Medicaid ~8% (~3.4M), legitimate cash (TrumpRx/direct) ~33% (~14M), imported or counterfeit ~7% (~3M). The income gap widened because the bottom third depends more on the gray market and lost Medicaid opt-ins. Adult obesity is ~34.8% (down from 36.4%). About 25% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug, mostly uninsured, on Medicaid in non-covering states, or older adults priced out after December 2027. The 65+ figure rose to ~14% under the Bridge pilot (mid-2027), then fell back to ~12% after it lapsed. Under-18 use is concentrated in ages 12–17; about 1 in 5 adolescents with severe obesity in upper-income households is on a drug.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot ended Dec 2027; Congress did not extend it after CBO scored a permanent benefit at ~$41B over 2028–2037. Pilot arithmetic: peak enrolment ~1.3M × $245 × 12 ≈ $3.8B annualised; with ramp-up, ~$4.2B across 18 months. After it lapsed, an estimated ~0.5M kept Part D coverage under cardiovascular, CKD, sleep-apnoea or diabetes codes, ~0.35M moved to cash (~$299–349/month), and ~0.45M stopped. From Aug 2028, tirzepatide's dementia-risk label opens a new Part D route under prior authorisation. Medicaid: 14 states opted in at the $245 rate in 2027; 5 have since dropped out because of budget pressure from the 2027 Medicaid changes.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide costs $6–40/month and has 60+ brands. Canadian generics are CAD 70–110. Generics are approved in Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, China and much of the Gulf, about 170 countries in all. India and China are now the volume source for most of the world's semaglutide.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Employers covering weight management fell 60% → 44% (Business Group on Health, 2028), and another 9% cover only through monitored 'metabolic tracks' with adherence verification. Coverage now concentrates on diabetes and cardiac codes, and BMI ≥35 thresholds are common. Orals were ~52% of new starts by Q2 2028 but still under 40% of total users, because established injectable users stay put. Cash prices: Wegovy pill $149 for starting doses and $299 for maintenance; Foundayo $149–349; injectables via TrumpRx ~$299–449 after manufacturers withdrew some of the 2025 intro discounts when the Medicare volume deal ended. The gray market is mostly mail-order Indian and Chinese semaglutide vials and counterfeit pens, about 3M users. Despite FDA import alerts, personal-importation enforcement is weak.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Mar 2027)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: cardiovascular risk reduction (semaglutide, 2024; tirzepatide, 2028 on SURMOUNT-MMO)
reduction of risk of all-cause dementia in adults with obesity and established cardiovascular disease (tirzepatide, Aug 2028; postmarketing confirmatory trial required)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol reduction: heavily prescribed off-label via telehealth and increasingly encouraged by employer EAPs; oral semaglutide AUD phase 3 under way
dementia-prevention use by people without cardiovascular disease, especially 55–70-year-olds with a family history, cash-paid on orals
microdosing for 'metabolic health' and 'steadiness', now partly employer-adjacent
nicotine, gambling and compulsive-shopping reduction: observational support, no approvals
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: The driver asked for an oral that matches injectables; the approval rules allow it only as a new form of an existing product, so it arrived as a head-to-head result. In Jun 2027 a 72-week trial found the Wegovy pill 25 mg non-inferior to injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg (~15.1% vs ~15.6%), and the label was updated. Orforglipron is close to it. No oral matches tirzepatide yet. The dementia indication came from a tirzepatide sNDA based on a prespecified cognitive substudy of SURMOUNT-MMO. It got priority review and a 9–7 advisory committee vote. Semaglutide's EVOKE failure in established Alzheimer's still frames the dispute. CagriSema was approved Mar 2027; uptake is modest because it lost to tirzepatide. Retatrutide's BLA was filed Feb 2027 and the decision was extended to Q1 2029 over dysesthesia and discontinuation data, so it is not on the US market. Amycretin is in phase 3, with filing planned for 2029. Survodutide was filed Jun 2028, so a decision is due no earlier than mid-2029. MariTide (monthly) is not on the market. Bimagrumab-type muscle-preserving adjuncts are in phase 2/3; none is approved. Global incretin market ~$118B (2027). US net prices are rising slightly; volume growth comes from ex-US generics.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Orals have similar GI profiles, with more early-escalation nausea on Foundayo.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; unchanged.
No causal confirmation from the larger outcome trials; absolute risk low. Litigation largely consolidated.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: A 2028 Medicare claims cohort (n≈1.9M) found hip-fracture hazard ratio ~1.3 among users aged 65+ after more than 2 years of continuous use, versus matched non-users with similar weight loss from other causes. DXA substudies show 2–4% hip BMD loss in older long-term users. Sarcopenia diagnoses in users aged 70+ roughly doubled from 2025. Risk is concentrated in older women, people taking little protein, and repeated cyclers who regain fat but not muscle.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class safety labelling change (Jul 2028): bone and lean-mass warning, protein and resistance-training counselling, and DXA consideration for patients 65+ before and after 12 months. Endocrine Society/AACE joint guidance. CMS added a DXA coverage code for incretin users 65+.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Further cohorts are still conflicting; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA added it to adverse reactions in 2027 without a class warning.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The first large pragmatic cohort using a validated anhedonia scale (2027, n≈22k) found a clinically meaningful rise in ~7% of users versus ~3% of matched controls. The effect is dose-related and partly reverses on dose reduction. Prospective trial data are still missing. The same mechanism is now marketed through the alcohol-use and dementia narratives.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA requested a postmarketing observational study (2028); no labelling.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Real-world 2027–28 data settle nearer half to two-thirds regain within 18 months, worse after repeated cycles. Cyclers who regain do so disproportionately as fat, which feeds the lean-mass problem.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly; used to justify chronic-therapy framing and employer adherence monitoring.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: More case series of B12, iron and vitamin D deficiency, especially among people taking low doses outside clinical care.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Included in 2028 professional guidance; no label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of follow-up exists. The bone signal raises specific concern about adolescents not reaching peak bone mass; no data.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric bone-density postmarketing requirement added to the 2028 adolescent oral approval.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: By mid-2028 there were ~6,400 FDA adverse-event reports tied to non-FDA-approved product. The Feb 2028 CDC advisory linked an endotoxin-contaminated imported vial lot to 41 hospitalisations and 2 deaths across 5 states. Mg/unit confusion with reconstituted vials is the most common dosing error, with poison-centre calls up ~3× since 2025.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA import alert on unapproved semaglutide/tirzepatide; CBP mail seizures; states suing marketplaces. Personal-importation enforcement remains weak.

food_and_beverage.state: About 30% of US households have a user. Snack and confectionery volumes are down ~4–6% from 2025 and sugary-drink volume ~5%. Price increases and protein, fibre and smaller-pack lines keep dollar sales roughly flat. Mondelez and Hershey have trimmed SKUs, and 'GLP-1 friendly' is now a commodity label. Protein-fortified products are the fastest-growing aisle. Volume pressure is largest in middle-income suburbs.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down ~7% from 2025 and beer ~4%. Employer EAP-driven off-label alcohol use has cut demand among the heaviest drinkers, who account for most sales. Diageo and Brown-Forman have closed some US distilling capacity and pushed non-alcoholic lines and premium 'occasion' pours. On-premise bar hours are shrinking in mid-sized cities.

restaurants.state: Traffic is broadly flat. Average check is under pressure, offset by small-plate and protein menus (Olive Garden, Chili's lighter-portion menus are now permanent). Buffet and all-you-can-eat formats are closing. Dessert attach rates are down, sour and spicy items are up.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking: Torrid's store count is down about a third from 2024, and DXL has merged its formats. Mainstream retailers have finished the size-down re-buying wave and now face a 'regain' market of shoppers cycling between sizes, which pushes stretch fabrics and rental.

fitness.state: Strength training is the growth market: Planet Fitness and regional chains have turned cardio floor into racks. DXA and body-composition scanning chains are expanding after the bone and muscle warnings. Employer 'metabolic tracks' bundle gym-check-ins with adherence.

insurance.state: Employers covering weight management fell to 44%. Pharmacy trend was ~+9% in 2028. Coverage is concentrated on diabetes, cardiovascular, sleep-apnoea and now dementia codes, behind prior authorisation. Outcomes-based wellness premium differentials of up to 30% tied to BMI or verified adherence have spread among large self-insured employers. PBMs sell adherence-verification as a product. Medicare actuaries are watching the dementia label nervously.

pharma.state: Lilly and Novo still dominate the US. Net US prices ticked up after the Medicare deal lapsed and some cash discounts were withdrawn, while ex-US prices collapse under generics. Orals widen the market, and dementia gives Lilly a new Medicare channel. Counterfeits are a brand-protection cost line. Indian and Chinese generic makers are the volume story outside the US.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A lean, slightly soft body in someone over 40 reads as 'on it'. A lean, muscular one reads as 'on it and lifting'. In middle-income workplaces, a visibly regained body now reads as someone whose coverage lapsed.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Two tiers have hardened. The insured and cash-rich take branded orals with DXA scans and protein coaching. Lower-income users take mail-order vials of uncertain strength, or nothing. Older adults who lost the Bridge pilot are a visible cohort of regainers. Upper-income adolescents are the most medicated youth group.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are shorter and smaller. 'Food noise' is everyday language. Fasting has been reclaimed by Christian and Muslim congregations as something done without a drug: the 'Bread Alone' fast network that started in Tulsa churches claims 300 congregations. Thanksgiving coverage now runs 'how to host a table where half the guests aren't hungry'.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating apps let users mark 'on GLP-1' or 'off'. Some users report choosing partners on the same schedule. Couples therapists describe 'desire mismatch' between an on-drug partner and an off-drug partner as a common presenting issue.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has split into two moral readings. Clinics and employers frame it as noise to be regulated. A noisy counter-movement frames it as a sign of being alive: fat-acceptance revivalists, 'natural' MAHA-adjacent influencers, church fasting groups, and the Philadelphia- and Brooklyn-based 'Unmuted' artists' collective. They agree on little except refusal.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Measured in ~7% of users versus ~3% of controls in a 2027 cohort, dose-related. Many more users report a milder 'evenness' that they and their employers describe positively.
interior_life.framing: Institutions call it a feature and name it 'steadiness'. HR materials for monitored metabolic tracks cite lower absenteeism, fewer conflict incidents and lower turnover among adherent enrollees. Clinicians call it a side effect. The Unmuted collective calls it sedation. Most users call it nothing.
interior_life.effect_on_work: About 3M employees sit in adherence-verified programmes, mostly in call centres, logistics, back-office finance and state employee plans. A widely cited 2028 HR-analytics study found adherent enrollees had ~12% lower voluntary turnover. That is confounded by health and income, but it is used anyway. Managers informally prefer 'steady' hires. EEOC has two pending ADA charges arguing premium differentials penalise people who discontinued for side effects.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Sportsbooks report lower wagering among identifiable users. Late-night bar and club hours have shrunk in mid-sized cities. Sour, spicy and loud foods and music are a genre. The Unmuted collective holds 'off nights' where performers skip a dose. A minor literary wave of 'flat' fiction is reviewed as either profound or numb.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Desire mismatch is common in therapy rooms. Some couples synchronise dosing schedules, and some users take drug holidays around anniversaries and holidays, which feeds cycling.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Coalition politics more than mood. A left–right alliance of fat-acceptance groups, labour advocates, MAHA-aligned state legislators and religious fasting movements backs bills limiting adherence-conditioned premiums. Illinois passed one, and California's is pending. Pundits claiming a 'sedated electorate' have no evidence. Turnout data show nothing measurable.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-speed on approvals: priority review for the dementia sNDA and quick updating of the oral label. Hard-line on imports in rhetoric, with import alerts and CBP mail seizures, but personal importation remains porous. HHS rhetoric is split between MAHA 'food first' messaging and the administration's own pharma deals.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The Medicare Bridge pilot lapsed Dec 2027 and was not extended. TrumpRx cash prices continue. Federal tri-agency guidance (Sep 2027) confirmed that wellness programmes may tie up to a 30% premium differential to verified pharmacy-fill adherence or BMI outcomes, with a reasonable-alternative standard.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Adherence is monitored through PBM fill data and app-linked pill and pen logs shared with wellness vendors under consent forms. Five state employee health plans, including Texas and Indiana, cover weight-loss GLP-1s only through monitored tracks. Two state Medicaid programmes tie continued coverage to documented adherence and BMI progress at 6 and 12 months.
state.workforce_or_military: DoD TRICARE covers incretins for weight management only for diabetes or cardiac codes. The Army pilots supervised oral use for recruits within 10% of the weight standard. Trucking firms encourage off-label alcohol-reduction use; DOT has not ruled on it.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: India and China supply most of the world's semaglutide. US–India trade talks include CBP enforcement on mail-order generics. Danish and US politicians spar over US prices running ~30× Indian generic prices. Manufacturers trade US price concessions for tariff treatment.

events.event: Head-to-head trial finds Wegovy pill 25 mg non-inferior to injectable semaglutide; FDA updates label; orals pass half of US new starts within a year

Labor, HHS and Treasury guidance lets employer wellness programmes tie up to 30% premium differentials to fill-verified GLP-1 adherence or BMI; Business Group on Health finds 44% of employers now cover weight loss, many only via monitored tracks
Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot expires after Congress declines a $41B extension; ~1.3M beneficiaries lose the $50 copay, and manufacturers withdraw some TrumpRx intro discounts
CDC health advisory links contaminated imported semaglutide vials to 41 hospitalisations and 2 deaths in five states; FDA issues import alert on unapproved incretins
After Medicare cohort shows ~30% higher hip-fracture risk in long-term users over 65, FDA orders class bone and lean-mass warning; CMS adds DXA coverage code
FDA approves tirzepatide to reduce dementia risk in adults with obesity and cardiovascular disease after a 9–7 advisory vote; neurologists dispute substudy basis

open_tensions: The dementia label pushes the drug toward the oldest users just as the bone and muscle warning says they are most harmed by it, and Medicare, having just let the Bridge pilot lapse, is now paying for it through a different door.

Adherence-conditioned premiums reward continuous use while the evidence says cycling is the norm and blunting is real in a minority. EEOC charges and state bans are testing whether 'steadiness' can be a condition of affordable insurance.
Three million Americans take mail-order product of uncertain strength because the US price is ~30× India's, and enforcement keeps losing to the mail.
Upper-income adolescents are growing up medicated through the years when peak bone mass forms, with no long-horizon data and a new bone warning on the label.

prose.headline: The Steady Workforce: Your Premium Now Depends on Your Pill. Your Mother Just Lost Hers. Your Son Buys His From Hyderabad.
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 about one American adult in six is taking an incretin drug, and more than one in five has tried one. Mostly that now means a pill. Last year a head-to-head trial showed daily oral semaglutide doing what the weekly pen does. That ended the needle as a reason to say no, and orals became the way most people start. Starting doses still cost $149 through the government's cash channel. Maintenance doses run $299 and up. Wegovy's list price of $1,349 is still printed on boxes nobody pays for.

Who pays has stopped being a question and become a hierarchy. Fewer than half of large employers still cover the drugs for weight loss. Most coverage now runs through codes for diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease and, since August, dementia risk. Some of the employers who kept paying changed the terms. Federal guidance last autumn confirmed that a wellness programme can tie up to thirty percent of an employee's premium to proof that the prescription was filled and taken. Call centres, logistics firms and five state employee plans now run 'metabolic tracks.' Their HR decks cite lower absenteeism and turnover among the adherent and call the quality steadiness. A large cohort study found clinically meaningful flattening of pleasure in about seven percent of users, against three percent of comparable non-users. Few HR decks mention it.

The Medicare pilot that gave older Americans the drugs for a $50 copay ended in December, when Congress balked at the ten-year bill. Some of those 1.3 million beneficiaries found their way back through cardiac codes. Others pay cash, and almost half a million simply stopped, and are regaining. The regain is worse than the scale shows. In July the FDA put a bone and muscle warning on the whole class after Medicare claims showed long-term users over sixty-five breaking hips about thirty percent more often. A month later the agency approved tirzepatide to reduce dementia risk in older adults with obesity and heart disease, on a split advisory vote and a substudy neurologists are still arguing over. Geriatricians now spend appointments weighing a possible brain benefit against a measurable skeleton cost, with DXA scans Medicare has only just agreed to pay for.

Below the insured tier is the mail. Indian generic semaglutide costs less per month than a takeout lunch, and around three million Americans take vials of it, or of something that claims to be it. In February the CDC traced a contaminated lot to forty-one hospitalisations and two deaths across five states. Poison-centre calls about doses mixed up between milligrams and units have tripled. The FDA's import alert slows the packages and does not stop them.

The industries adapted rather than collapsed. Snack makers sell less volume at higher prices in smaller bags. Spirits volumes are down about seven percent, and some distilleries have shut. Plus-size chains keep closing stores. Gyms have pulled out treadmills to make room for squat racks. Restaurant traffic held, but dessert and late-night bar sales fell away in mid-sized cities.

The backlash is real, local and incoherent. In Philadelphia and Brooklyn the Unmuted collective holds performances where everyone skips a dose. In Tulsa, a church network teaches fasting as discipline rather than as something done to you. Fat-acceptance groups have revived alongside MAHA-aligned state legislators who distrust the pharma deals their own administration signed. Together they passed an Illinois ban on adherence-conditioned premiums. California may follow, and two complaints at the EEOC test whether discontinuing for side effects can cost you a raise. From the outside, the country looks healthier, calmer and thinner. Most of that is true.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Okafor, fifty-eight, logs in at 7:02 to the claims floor in Columbus. The pill is in her mouth before the badge reader beeps. The app pings green: day 311. Her premium stays at the steady rate.

The first caller is shouting about a denied MRI. Denise listens the way you listen to rain. She used to go home with these voices in her shoulders. Now they slide off. Her supervisor calls it a gift. Denise doesn't call it anything.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and forgets the other half until three. A coworker passes around sour gummies and everyone takes two.

Her mother calls at four. The Bridge thing ended, and the pharmacy wanted three hundred and nine dollars. She stopped in January. Her slacks are tight again, she says, and she fell in the driveway, just a sprain. The doctor wants a bone scan and mentioned the new dementia pill, maybe, if Medicare approves it, if her heart counts. Denise writes down DXA on a Post-it.

Dinner is chicken and green beans. Her son Marcus, twenty-six, comes over and drops a padded envelope on the counter: Hyderabad, ten milliliters, forty dollars. He's pulling up the units on a YouTube chart. She watches him tap the syringe twice.

"Check it again," she says.

"I checked it."

She used to fight him about things. She notices she isn't going to. She notices that she's noticing, and that it doesn't hurt.

At nine her husband asks if she wants to go dancing Saturday, like before. She says sure. She means it the way you mean weather.
